tracks.tagline: Design a mobile app that lets students order canteen food ahead and skip the queue.

1.title: User Research and Problem Statement
1.goal: Talk to real students about canteen queues, turn what you hear into a persona and a clear problem statement, and map the ordering flow. Good design starts with understanding people, not with screens.
learn: Planning and running short user interviews
Creating a persona from real findings
steps: Write 6-8 open-ended interview questions, such as 'Tell me about the last time you bought food at the canteen.'
Interview 3-5 students for 10 minutes each, or run a short Google Form survey with at least 15 responses.
Write each finding on a sticky note in a [FigJam](https://www.figma.com) board and group similar notes together.
Create one persona with a name, goals, frustrations and a quote taken from your research.
Write a problem statement in the form 'Students need a way to ___ because ___.'
Draw a user flow from opening the app to picking up the order, including one alternate path such as an item being sold out.
Share the FigJam link and write a short summary of your top 3 insights.
deliverables: Interview questions and notes or survey results
done_when: At least 3 interviews or 15 survey responses are recorded
Findings are grouped into at least 3 themes
The persona includes goals, frustrations and a real quote
The user flow covers the full order journey plus one alternate path
hints: Ask about past behaviour, not opinions; 'What did you do?' is better than 'Would you use...?'
Avoid leading questions such as 'Don't you hate long queues?'
Keep the persona based on what you heard, not on guesses.
1.stretch: Visit the canteen at peak time, time the queue and add these observations to your research.
post_highlights: Interviewed students to understand canteen queue problems
Created a research-based persona and problem statement
Mapped the full pre-order user flow in FigJam

2.title: Low-fidelity Wireframes
2.goal: Turn your user flow into grayscale wireframes for the main screens. Wireframes let you test layout and flow quickly before spending time on colours and details.
learn: Using frames and basic shapes in Figma
Sketching multiple ideas before choosing one
Linking wireframes to the user flow
steps: Sketch 2-3 paper versions of the menu screen and pick the one that best solves your problem statement.
In [Figma](https://www.figma.com), create a mobile frame and build wireframes for: home, menu, item details, cart, checkout and order status.
Use only gray boxes, simple text and placeholder icons; no colours or images yet.
Place the most important action on each screen where the thumb can reach it easily.
Arrange the screens left to right in flow order and label each one.
Show the wireframes to one classmate and note anything that confused them.
deliverables: Figma file with at least 6 wireframe screens
Short notes on feedback from one person
done_when: At least 6 screens cover the full flow from Week 1
Each screen has one clear primary action
Screens are in grayscale with no final visual styling
At least one change was made based on feedback
hints: Use Figma's mobile frame presets so your screens have realistic sizes.
Real content labels such as 'Masala Dosa - Rs 40' reveal layout problems better than 'Lorem ipsum'.
Search 'low fidelity wireframe examples' for reference before starting.
2.stretch: Add wireframes for an empty cart and an item-sold-out state.
post_highlights: Sketched and compared multiple layout ideas on paper
Built 6 low-fidelity wireframes in Figma for a canteen pre-order app
Improved the flow based on early feedback

3.title: High-fidelity UI and Mini Design System
3.goal: Create a small design system with colours, a type scale and reusable components, then use it to turn your wireframes into polished screens. You will also check basic accessibility.
learn: Auto layout for flexible buttons and cards
Basic accessibility: colour contrast and tap target size
steps: Pick a primary colour, a neutral palette and one accent, and save them as colour styles.
Define a type scale of 4-5 sizes (for example 12, 14, 16, 20, 28) and save them as text styles.
Build components with auto layout: button, menu item card, input field, and bottom navigation.
Add button variants for default, pressed and disabled states.
Rebuild all 6 screens using only your styles and components.
Check text contrast with a Figma contrast plugin and make tap targets at least 44x44 pt.
Create a 'Design System' page in the file that shows all styles and components.
deliverables: Design System page with colours, type and components
done_when: All colours and text on screens use saved styles
At least 4 reusable components exist, one with variants
Buttons and cards use auto layout
Body text meets a 4.5:1 contrast ratio
Tap targets are at least 44x44 pt
hints: Change a component's main copy and confirm every instance updates; if not, you detached it.
Use an 8-point spacing system (8, 16, 24, 32) for consistent layouts.
The [WCAG overview from W3C](https://www.w3.org/WAI/) explains contrast requirements.
3.stretch: Create a dark mode version of two screens using the same components.
post_highlights: Built a mini design system with colour styles, a type scale and components
Designed 6 high-fidelity screens using auto layout
Checked colour contrast and tap target sizes for accessibility

4.title: Prototype, Usability Test and Case Study
4.goal: Link your screens into a clickable prototype, test it with 3 people, fix the biggest issues and write a case study. This shows your full process from research to tested design.
steps: Connect all screens in Figma's Prototype tab so a user can place an order from start to finish.
Write 3 tasks for testers, such as 'Order a dosa and a tea for pickup at 1 pm.'
Test with 3 people, ask them to think aloud and note where they hesitate or make mistakes.
List all issues, rank them by how many testers hit them and fix the top 3.
Write a case study on Notion, Medium or Behance covering problem, research, wireframes, UI, testing and changes.
Record a 60-second screen video of the final prototype.
done_when: A tester can complete an order in the prototype without help
3 usability tests are documented with issues found
At least 3 issues are fixed and shown before and after
The case study covers every stage from research to testing
hints: During testing, stay quiet and let the tester struggle a little; that is where the insights are.
Use 'Smart animate' sparingly; clear flows matter more than fancy transitions.
Start the case study with the problem and the result, then show the process.
4.stretch: Measure task completion time for each tester before and after your fixes.
post_highlights: Built a clickable Figma prototype for a canteen pre-order app
Ran usability tests with 3 students and fixed the top issues
Published a full UX case study from research to tested design

tracks.tagline: Design a friendly mobile app that helps students build and keep daily habits.

1.title: Understanding Habit Struggles
1.goal: Research why students start and abandon habits, then create a persona, problem statement and user flow. This keeps your design focused on real needs instead of adding every feature you can think of.
steps: Write 6-8 open-ended questions about habits students have tried and why they stopped.
Interview 3-5 people or collect at least 15 survey responses.
Group findings into themes on a [FigJam](https://www.figma.com) board.
Look at 2 existing habit apps and note one thing each does well and one thing that frustrates users.
Create a persona and write a problem statement based on your strongest theme.
Draw a user flow for adding a new habit and checking it off each day.
deliverables: Persona, problem statement and user flow
done_when: At least 3 interviews or 15 survey responses are recorded
Findings are grouped into at least 3 themes
The problem statement is based on a research theme
The user flow covers adding and completing a habit
hints: Ask 'Tell me about the last habit you tried to build' to get real stories.
Competitor reviews on app stores are a free source of user frustrations.
Pick one core problem; a focused app is easier to design well.
1.stretch: Create a second persona with a different motivation and note how their flow differs.
post_highlights: Researched why students struggle to keep habits
Reviewed existing habit apps to find gaps
Created a persona, problem statement and user flow in FigJam

2.title: Wireframing the Core Screens
2.goal: Create grayscale wireframes for the main screens of your habit tracker. Focus on making adding and checking off a habit fast and obvious.
learn: Frames, shapes and grids in Figma
steps: Sketch 2-3 paper versions of the home screen showing today's habits.
In [Figma](https://www.figma.com), build wireframes for: onboarding, home, add habit, habit details and weekly progress.
Keep everything grayscale and use real labels like 'Drink 8 glasses of water'.
Make checking off a habit possible with a single tap on the home screen.
Arrange screens in flow order with labels.
Get feedback from one person and write down what you changed.
deliverables: Figma file with at least 5 wireframe screens
done_when: At least 5 screens cover the flow from Week 1
A habit can be checked off in one tap on the home screen
Screens are grayscale with no final styling
At least one change was made from feedback
hints: Use a layout grid on your frames to keep spacing consistent.
Keep onboarding to 3 screens or fewer.
If you cannot explain a screen's purpose in one sentence, simplify it.
2.stretch: Wireframe an empty state for a new user with no habits yet.
post_highlights: Explored multiple home screen layouts through paper sketches
Wireframed 5 core screens for a habit tracker in Figma
Designed one-tap habit check-off based on user needs

3.title: Visual Design and Components
3.goal: Define a small design system and apply it to create high-fidelity screens. You will learn how components and styles keep a design consistent and easy to update.
steps: Choose a calm colour palette and save primary, neutral, success and error colours as styles.
Set up a type scale of 4-5 text styles.
Build components with auto layout: habit row, checkbox, button, progress ring or bar, and tab bar.
Add variants for the habit row: not done, done and missed.
Rebuild all wireframe screens using your components.
Check contrast and make sure tap targets are at least 44x44 pt.
Document everything on a 'Design System' page.
done_when: All screens use saved colour and text styles
The habit row component has at least 3 variants
Buttons and rows use auto layout
Body text meets a 4.5:1 contrast ratio and tap targets are at least 44x44 pt
hints: Do not rely on colour alone to show 'done'; add a checkmark icon too.
Use an 8-point spacing system.
Name layers and components clearly so your file is easy to share.
3.stretch: Design a streak celebration screen that stays accessible and not distracting.
post_highlights: Created a design system with styles and reusable components
Designed high-fidelity habit tracker screens using auto layout
Applied accessibility checks for contrast and tap targets

4.title: Prototype, Testing and Case Study
4.goal: Build a clickable prototype, run usability tests with 3 people, iterate on the design and publish a case study. This completes your first end-to-end UX project.
steps: Link screens in Figma so users can add a habit, check it off and view weekly progress.
Write 3 realistic test tasks.
Test with 3 people, ask them to think aloud and note problems.
Rank issues by frequency and severity and fix the top 3.
Write a case study covering problem, research, wireframes, UI, testing and iteration.
Record a 60-second prototype walkthrough.
done_when: All 3 test tasks can be completed in the prototype
3 tests are documented
At least 3 issues are fixed with before/after evidence
The case study covers every stage of the process
hints: Ask testers 'What do you expect will happen if you tap this?' before they tap.
Keep the case study visual: one image per section.
Mention what you would do next if you had more time.
4.stretch: Add a simple interaction such as a checkbox animation using Figma's interactive components.
post_highlights: Built and tested a clickable habit tracker prototype with 3 users
Iterated on the design to fix the top usability issues
Published a complete UX case study

tracks.tagline: Redesign the website of a local business such as a clinic, coaching centre or cafe so customers find what they need faster.

1.title: Audit and Research
1.goal: Pick a local business with an outdated website, audit what is not working and talk to people who might use it. A redesign is only useful if you know which problems to fix.
learn: Running a heuristic review of an existing site
steps: Choose a local clinic, coaching centre, cafe or shop whose website you find hard to use.
Take screenshots of the key pages and mark problems such as unclear navigation, small text or missing contact details.
Rate the site against 5 of Nielsen's usability heuristics and note one example for each.
Interview 3 people or survey at least 15 about what they look for on such a website.
Create a persona and a problem statement.
Draw a user flow for the most common task, such as booking an appointment or finding opening hours.
deliverables: Annotated screenshots of the current site
User flow for the main task
done_when: At least 5 issues are identified on the current site
At least 3 interviews or 15 survey responses are recorded
The problem statement links to your findings
The user flow covers one complete task
hints: Search 'Nielsen 10 usability heuristics' for the list and examples.
Pick a site with clear room for improvement but not so large that the project gets out of hand.
This is a practice redesign; mention in your case study that it is an unofficial concept.
1.stretch: Time how long 2 people take to find a key piece of information on the current site.
post_highlights: Audited a local business website using usability heuristics
Interviewed potential users to understand their needs
Defined a persona, problem statement and user flow for the redesign

2.title: Information Architecture and Wireframes
2.goal: Reorganise the site's content into a clear structure and create grayscale wireframes for desktop and mobile. Good structure is the biggest improvement in most redesigns.
steps: List every piece of content on the current site and group it into logical pages.
Draw a new sitemap in [FigJam](https://www.figma.com) with no more than 5-6 top-level pages.
Wireframe the home page, the main task page and a contact page for desktop.
Create mobile versions of the same 3 pages.
Make the main task, such as 'Book appointment', reachable from the home page in one click.
Get feedback from one person and note your changes.
deliverables: At least 3 desktop and 3 mobile wireframes
done_when: The sitemap has no more than 6 top-level pages
Desktop and mobile wireframes exist for 3 pages
The main task is one click from the home page
At least one change was made from feedback
hints: Use the words your interviewees used as navigation labels.
Design mobile first if most users will visit on their phones.
Keep wireframes grayscale so feedback focuses on structure.
2.stretch: Run a quick card-sorting exercise with 2 people to validate your navigation groups.
post_highlights: Restructured a local business website with a new sitemap
Wireframed desktop and mobile versions of the key pages
Made the main customer task reachable in one click

3.title: High-fidelity Design System and Pages
3.goal: Build a small design system and use it to create polished desktop and mobile pages. You will learn how consistent components make responsive design easier.
learn: Layout grids for desktop and mobile
steps: Create a colour palette that fits the business and save it as styles.
Define a type scale that works on both desktop and mobile.
Set up a 12-column grid for desktop and a 4-column grid for mobile.
Build components with auto layout: navbar, button, service card, form field and footer.
Design the 3 pages at high fidelity for both desktop and mobile.
Check contrast and make mobile tap targets at least 44x44 pt.
Document everything on a 'Design System' page.
deliverables: 3 high-fidelity desktop pages and 3 mobile pages
done_when: All pages use saved styles and components
At least 5 components are built with auto layout
Pages follow the layout grids
Body text meets a 4.5:1 contrast ratio and tap targets are at least 44x44 pt
hints: Set auto layout children to 'Fill container' so cards stretch correctly.
Use real photos only if you have rights to them; placeholder images are fine.
The [WCAG overview from W3C](https://www.w3.org/WAI/) explains contrast basics.
3.stretch: Add a tablet layout for the home page.
post_highlights: Built a design system with responsive components
Designed high-fidelity desktop and mobile pages for a website redesign
Checked the design for colour contrast and tap target sizes

4.title: Prototype, Testing and Case Study
4.goal: Prototype the main task, test old versus new with 3 people and write a case study comparing the two. Showing measurable improvement makes your redesign convincing.
steps: Prototype the main task flow on mobile, such as booking an appointment.
Ask 3 people to do the same task on the old site and your prototype, and note time and problems.
Fix the top 3 issues found in your prototype.
Write a case study with before/after screenshots, test results and what you learned.
Label the project clearly as an unofficial concept redesign.
Record a 60-second walkthrough of the new flow.
done_when: The main task can be completed in the prototype without help
3 people tested both the old site and the prototype
At least 3 issues are fixed after testing
The case study includes before/after comparisons and test results
hints: Give testers the same task wording for both versions to keep the comparison fair.
Report simple numbers like average time or number of errors.
Show the business name only if you make clear the work is a concept.
4.stretch: Share the case study with the business owner and note their feedback.
post_highlights: Prototyped a redesigned booking flow for a local business website
Compared the old and new designs with 3 users and measured improvements
Published a before/after UX case study
